title: SQL and Rust Foundations Practice Contract
purpose: Turn resume-visible software skill claims into repeatable, evidence-backed practice with SQL as the primary lane, Rust as the secondary lane, and a small maintenance lane for other claimed technologies.

allocation.principle: Every study session includes typed retrieval or implementation; reading alone does not count as practice.

claimDefense.rule: A public skill claim is defensible only when the learner can reconstruct the named foundation without AI assistance, explain why it works, and pass the track mastery gates.

exercises.prompt: List open tasks ordered by highest priority then oldest creation time. Return only id, title, priority, created_at.
For each repository, count open tasks and return only repositories with at least three open tasks.
Explain, then demonstrate, the difference between WHERE and HAVING using task status and grouped repository counts.
Join tasks to projects and assignees. Diagnose how a many-to-many assignment table can multiply rows.
Return every project even when it has zero tasks, with an open_task_count of zero.
Find tasks without an assignee and produce a display owner using COALESCE without treating NULL as an empty string.
Using a CTE, find repositories whose average completed-task duration exceeds the global completed-task average.
Return the latest task event per task using ROW_NUMBER or an equivalent window pattern.
Rank repositories by open high-priority task count while preserving ties.
For each task, show its current event and previous event timestamp using LAG.
Move a task and its assignment atomically to a new project/agent; show the transaction and rollback path.
Design normalized tables for projects, tasks, agents, assignments, repositories, sprints, and task_events with keys and constraints.
Given frequent lookup by repository_id, status, and created_at, propose an index and explain read/write tradeoffs before checking the query plan.
Explain why adding an index can speed reads but slow inserts and updates; identify one case where an index is unlikely to help.
From an unfamiliar schema, inspect relationships and produce one join, one aggregate, one CTE, one window query, one safe update transaction, and one index recommendation without AI assistance.

masteryGates: Write multi-table joins from an unfamiliar schema without AI assistance.
Explain join cardinality and diagnose duplicate-row explosions.
Use GROUP BY/HAVING, a CTE, and a window function correctly.
Handle NULL intentionally and explain three-valued comparison behavior.
Perform a data change inside a transaction with a rollback path.
Design normalized tables with keys, constraints, and a many-to-many bridge.
Recommend an index and explain its query-plan and write-cost tradeoffs.

exercises.prompt: Write a function that parses a priority string into a numeric rank and returns a meaningful type.
Model TaskStatus as an enum and render a user-facing label with match.
Explain why moving a String invalidates the first binding and demonstrate one borrowing alternative.
Write a function that receives a task title by reference and computes a derived value without taking ownership.
Parse a task id and optional assignee from text, propagating errors with Result rather than panicking.
Group tasks by repository with HashMap and derive open counts using iterator adapters.
Define a small Renderable trait and implement it for two task-domain types.
Split a tiny task CLI domain into modules and add unit tests for parsing and status transitions.
Write and explain a function returning one of two borrowed labels; add the minimal lifetime annotation when inference cannot express the relationship.
Share a task counter across threads with Arc<Mutex<_>> and explain what Send and Sync protect conceptually.

masteryGates: Explain a String move and repair it with borrowing instead of reflexive cloning.
Use structs, enums, and match to model a small domain.
Use Option and Result without panic-driven control flow.
Write iterator-based transformations over Vec and HashMap.
Define and implement a trait with a useful generic bound.
Organize modules and pass cargo test.
Explain the purpose of lifetime annotations in a borrowed-return example.

integrationProject.name: taskq
integrationProject.goal: Build a tiny Rust CLI backed by SQLite so SQL and Rust practice converge in one bounded project.

weeklyCadence.focus: SQL joins, aggregation, and schema reasoning

sessionTemplate.activity: record confusion and next retrieval target

acceptanceContract.statement: SQL receives 50% of deliberate practice, Rust 25%, and resume-claim maintenance 25% until priorities are intentionally revised.
Every session includes typed retrieval, query writing, code, or explanation from memory; reading alone cannot satisfy a session.
SQL coverage includes filtering, aggregation, joins, NULL, CTEs/subqueries, windows, safe mutation, modeling, indexes, and query plans.
Rust coverage includes types, structs/enums, ownership, borrowing, Option/Result, collections/iterators, traits/generics, modules/tests, lifetimes, and concurrency foundations.
The taskq capstone converges Rust and SQLite instead of creating two unrelated toy tracks.
A resume-visible claim reaches defensible state only after no-AI reconstruction, explanation, and mastery-gate evidence.
